lessons.title: Breeding Goals and Target Product Profiles
lessons.requiredTeachingVisual: Breeding objective and target-product profile map
lessons.objective: Convert a broad breeding idea into measurable, prioritized traits, testing environments, product uses, and release criteria.
coreScience: A breeding program begins with a decision about what population should become better, for whom, and under which environments. “Higher quality,” “better yield,” or “strong genetics” are not testable objectives. A target product profile translates intended lawful use into measurable traits such as flowering response, maturity window, biomass or inflorescence yield, cannabinoid ratio, volatile profile, seed or fiber properties, architecture, disease response, environmental adaptation, uniformity, and postharvest performance.

Traits can conflict. Later maturity may raise yield in one environment but increase frost or disease exposure. Dense flowers may improve visual yield while increasing drying and microbial risk. High concentration in a small sample may not maximize total analyte yield per plant or per area. A useful profile therefore ranks must-have traits, desired traits, unacceptable traits, and tradeoffs. It also names the testing methods, units, sample positions, environments, and minimum evidence required.

The objective controls population design. A rare single-gene trait may require marker-assisted introgression and backcrossing; a highly quantitative trait may require large populations, replicated trials, family selection, and genomic prediction. The target must remain version-controlled because regulations, product standards, climates, and customer needs change. Changing the objective after observing the results creates biased selection and makes progress difficult to audit.
cultivationRelevance: Create the target product profile before making crosses. Use it to choose parents, population sizes, trial environments, laboratory panels, rejection rules, and release evidence.
measureAndRecord: Program ID and version; intended lawful use; target environments; trait definitions and units; minimum/optimum/maximum values; trait weights; unacceptable traits; testing methods; sample numbers; release and stop criteria; approver and revision history.
misconceptions: The best-looking plant is automatically the best breeding parent.
Every desired trait can be maximized at the same time.
A cultivar can be released from one successful grow.
evidenceLimits: Trait priorities, legal thresholds, market needs, and environmental risks are program-specific and must be refreshed before each release.

lessons.title: Parent Selection and Complementary Traits
lessons.objective: Select parents from verified identity, heritable performance, complementary strengths, diversity, fertility, and evidence quality rather than reputation alone.
coreScience: A parent contributes alleles, cytoplasm when used as the seed parent, and a sampling of its family history. The strongest individual phenotype is not always the best parent. Performance can reflect environment, position, crop load, disease escape, or measurement error, and a visually impressive clone may transmit little of the feature that made it desirable.

Parent selection should combine identity, pedigree, replicated phenotype, laboratory data, fertility, sex stability, disease status, and genetic relationship. Complementarity means that one parent supplies strengths missing from the other while neither introduces unacceptable liabilities. Two parents with the same weakness rarely solve it simply because their names or aromas differ. Conversely, extreme genetic distance can create useful variation but also disrupt favorable allele combinations and increase segregation.

Use family and progeny information when possible. A parent that repeatedly produces acceptable offspring across mates may have high general combining ability. A parent that performs unusually well with one specific mate may show specific combining ability. Molecular markers can confirm identity, sex genotype, major loci, and relationship, but they do not replace phenotype for traits not fully explained by those markers. Quarantine and pathogen testing are part of parent qualification because disease can be transmitted with living material and can distort trait evaluation.
cultivationRelevance: Create a parent dossier and a trait-complementarity matrix before flowering. Retain backup clones or verified seed, and document why each parent was chosen and what risk it introduces.
measureAndRecord: Parent ID and source; sex genotype and expression; pedigree and genotyping; health and pathogen status; replicated trait means and variation; chemotype and volatile data; fertility and pollen/seed quality; relationship estimate; strengths, weaknesses, risks, and backup location.
misconceptions: Crossing two elite plants guarantees elite offspring.
Unrelated parents are always superior to related parents.
A cultivar name proves genetic identity and parentage.
evidenceLimits: Breeding value and combining ability can only be estimated within defined populations, mates, environments, and measured traits.

lessons.title: Controlled Crosses and Parent Verification
lessons.objective: Preserve parent identity and prevent unintended pollen, sample, label, and generation errors during controlled crossing.
coreScience: A controlled cross is a documented transfer of pollen from a verified pollen parent to a verified seed parent while excluding unintended pollen. In Cannabis, wind-dispersed pollen, delayed pollen release, mixed tools, mislabeled clones, and overlooked male or intersexual flowers can compromise a cross. A physical bag or separate room is not sufficient unless airflow, timing, seals, handling, and later seed recovery are controlled.

Verification begins before flowering. Confirm parent IDs from permanent records and, when appropriate, genotype markers or fingerprints. Map every flowering plant, inspect for unexpected sex expression, and define pollen collection, storage, viability, and disposal methods. Pollinated branches or plants require durable cross labels tied to a cross record. Open-pollinated seed from a mixed room must not be represented as a known biparental cross.

After seed set, preserve maternal plant, branch or inflorescence position, pollination date, pollen lot, personnel, and harvest lot. Progeny testing or markers can detect some errors, but no marker panel proves complete parentage unless it is sufficiently informative for the candidate parents. Control plants and unpollinated checks help identify stray pollen. Failed identity or contamination control should downgrade the seed lot rather than be hidden by a confident name.
cultivationRelevance: Use one permanent cross ID from parent qualification through seed inventory and progeny trial. Separate breeding seed from production seed and preserve exceptions and uncertainty.
measureAndRecord: Cross ID; verified maternal and pollen parent IDs; genotype/identity method; flowering and isolation map; pollen lot, viability and collection date; pollination date/site; exclusion method; control plants; unexpected seed set; seed harvest lot; deviations and disposition.
misconceptions: Seed collected from a labeled female automatically has the intended father.
A closed door prevents Cannabis pollen movement.
evidenceLimits: Parentage confidence depends on isolation, candidate-parent set, marker informativeness, sampling, and record integrity.

lessons.title: F1 Populations and Heterozygosity
lessons.requiredTeachingVisual: F1 allele and heterozygosity concept diagram
lessons.objective: Interpret F1 uniformity, heterozygosity, dominance, maternal effects, and hybrid performance without assuming every F1 is identical or superior.
coreScience: The F1 generation is the first filial generation from two parents. At a locus where the parents are fixed for different alleles, every true F1 is heterozygous. Cannabis parents, however, are often highly heterozygous rather than fully inbred. Their F1 offspring can therefore segregate at many loci and may vary substantially even though they share the same two named parents.

Uniform F1 hybrids usually require stable, sufficiently homozygous or otherwise predictable parental lines. Heterosis is performance above a defined parental reference, not simply vigor in a healthy seedling. It can arise from dominance, overdominance, epistasis, masking of deleterious alleles, and population divergence. Hybrid vigor in one environment or trait does not prove superior quality, stability, fertility, or transmission.

Reciprocal crosses can differ because the seed parent contributes cytoplasm, seed size, maternal environment, and early developmental effects. Parent sex also changes which chromosomes and recombination histories can be transmitted in dioecious material. Evaluate both reciprocal directions when the program depends on seed traits, vigor, flowering, or chemistry and when lawful logistics permit. F1 records must distinguish a single selected F1 clone from the entire F1 family.
cultivationRelevance: Do not market a variable F1 family as uniform without data. Measure within-family variance and preserve individual IDs for selected F1 plants.
measureAndRecord: Cross and reciprocal direction; parent heterozygosity and relatedness; F1 population size; germination and vigor; trait mean and within-family variance; parental and check performance; heterosis calculation and reference; fertility, sex and off-types.
misconceptions: All F1 seed from two parents is genetically identical.
F1 always means uniform and vigorous.
A selected F1 clone describes every seed in the F1 lot.
evidenceLimits: F1 variation depends on parental heterozygosity, allele phase, relatedness, cytoplasm, seed environment, and trait architecture.

lessons.title: F2 Segregation and Population Size
lessons.objective: Design F2 populations around trait architecture, recombination, linkage, rare-combination probability, and selection capacity.
coreScience: An F2 population is commonly produced by selfing or intercrossing F1 individuals. It exposes new homozygous and recombinant combinations, making it valuable for mapping and selection. Simple 1:2:1 or 3:1 expectations apply only under defined single-locus assumptions with clear phenotypes, adequate sample size, no distortion, and reliable classification. Most horticultural traits involve multiple loci, dominance, epistasis, linkage, genotype-by-environment interaction, and measurement error.

Population size should be based on the probability of the desired combination and the number of individuals that can be measured accurately. Recovering several independent favorable alleles in one individual can require far more plants than intuition suggests. Linkage can make combinations harder or easier to recover depending on allele phase and recombination distance. Selecting too few plants creates a genetic bottleneck and can fix hidden defects.

F2 individuals should be permanently identified and, where possible, preserved by clone or seed family before destructive testing. Selection can target individuals, but traits with low heritability often need F3 family confirmation. The rarest-looking phenotype is not automatically transgressive or heritable. Compare against parents and checks under the same conditions, and retain unselected or less selected material when conservation of diversity is part of the objective.
cultivationRelevance: Calculate a minimum population from trait probabilities, then increase it for mortality, sex ratio, testing losses, recombination uncertainty, and the need for multiple selected families.
measureAndRecord: F1 source and mating; F2 seed lot; planned and emerged population; trait model and expected frequency; sex and survival; phenotype distributions; genotypes/markers; family preservation; selected count and intensity; reasons for discard.
misconceptions: A small F2 shows every possible phenotype.
All F2 ratios follow one-gene Mendelian expectations.
The most extreme F2 plant will breed true.
evidenceLimits: Expected ratios and recovery probabilities depend on correct genetic models, linkage, penetrance, environment, sampling, viability, and classification.
